name: West Elm
sells: Only through its own stores and site (Williams-Sonoma family).
why: Mostly in-house designs, plus named collaborations like the Emma Chamberlain collection.
watch: Collab pieces are limited editions and sell out. Sitewide sales come around often, so a full-price item can usually wait.

name: Zara Home
sells: Its own stores and site; many lamps also appear on zara.com at the same price.
why: Quick, inexpensive takes on current looks, with no credited designers.
watch: Some pieces are stock factory designs sold by many brands (the cordless mushroom lamp is one). Reverse-search before paying Zara's price.

name: Urban Outfitters
sells: UO Home pieces are UO-only. UO MRKT listings are other brands selling through UO.
why: UO Home designs its own kits and lamps; the free UO Rewards membership often takes 40% off in the cart.
watch: Check "Sold by" on the page: UO MRKT items (like the Brightech Luna Drop) are often "Price as Marked" and skip promos. Other renamed items (the Otto) are mass-market brands under a UO name.

name: Brightech
sells: Its own site plus Target, Amazon, Home Depot, UO and others.
why: Los Angeles LED lighting brand with consistent, clean designs.
watch: Same lamp at near-identical prices everywhere; brightech.com tends to be cheapest and has the longest warranty.

name: JONATHAN Y
sells: Mostly as a third-party seller on Target, Walmart, Overstock and Kohl's.
why: Low-cost lamps that reinterpret popular looks.
watch: Wood, marble and rattan looks are often resin or printed finishes. Prices swing a lot between marketplaces.

name: Adesso
sells: Wholesale to many stores, which often rename its lamps.
why: Solid, simple lamps; the Orchard is real wood.
watch: Renamed by retailers (UO's Otto is the Adesso Orchard). Search the model number to compare.

name: Crosley Furniture
sells: Wholesale across big retailers and furniture sites.
why: Mid-century-leaning case goods at accessible prices.
watch: Renamed and repriced by retailers; some block promos with "Price as Marked".

name: Surya (Livabliss)
sells: Trade wholesaler; you buy through AllModern, Wayfair and other retailers.
why: Huge in-house range of rugs, lighting and decor.
watch: Retailers rename its pieces (AllModern's Keira is the Livabliss Desota). You can't buy direct.

name: Anthropologie
sells: Its own stores and site (URBN, Urban Outfitters' sister brand).
why: The closest step up from UO: an in-house design studio plus exclusive lighting collaborations, like Merve Kahraman's colorful glass lamps and Matilda Goad's scalloped lamps.
watch: It also resells other brands. Look for "Exclusively for Anthropologie" on the page to know it's their own.

name: Pooky
sells: Its US site and its New York design center showroom.
why: British lighting brand built on colorful, pleated and patterned shades you mix and match with bases. Shades are handmade in its own factory in India.
watch: The US and UK sites are separate, so order from the US one. Shades and bases are bought separately.

name: Matilda Goad & Co.
sells: Its US site, plus collaborations at Anthropologie and Liberty.
why: The brand that started the scalloped lampshade wave; if you like the UO Scallop kit, this is the original look.
watch: Many shades are sold without a base; check the fitting (US washer vs bulb clip) before buying.

name: Schoolhouse
sells: Its own site and Portland flagship (owned by Food52).
why: Vintage-inspired American lighting drawn by an in-house team, much of it assembled in its Portland factory.
watch: Mostly hardwired fixtures and pricier than the brands above; the Benchmade line is the most made-in-Portland.

name: Rejuvenation
sells: Its own stores and site (West Elm's sister brand at Williams-Sonoma).
why: Designs in Portland and makes most hardwired lighting there; vintage reproductions in solid brass.
watch: Best for ceiling and wall lights you'll keep for years; lamps are a smaller part of the range.

name: H&M Home
sells: Online in the US, plus some stores.
why: Same fast-fashion model as Zara Home and often cheaper, with in-house lamps and occasional designer collabs (Kelly Wearstler).
watch: Like Zara, some lamps are stock factory designs. Popular pieces sell out and restock unpredictably.

name: Mango Home
why: Zara Home's closest rival: marble, rattan and metal table lamps at low prices.
watch: Its "tactile metal table lamp" is the same generic cordless mushroom shape as Zara's, so the same reverse-search rule applies.

name: CB2
sells: Its own stores and site (Crate & Barrel's modern brand).
why: Exclusive pieces from a roster of independent studios, celebrity collabs and mid-century reissues.
watch: Free shipping only on items marked for it; collabs rotate out.

name: HAY
sells: Its own site and many design shops.
why: The next tier up: every lamp is credited to a named designer (Inga Sempé's pleated Matin, Naoto Fukasawa's Pao), at prices near West Elm's.
watch: Popular designs like the Matin are widely copied, so buy from HAY or an authorized dealer.

name: Lulu and Georgia
why: Designer collaborations (Sarah Sherman Samuel, Huey Lightshop) and in-house exclusives with a warm, collected look.
watch: It also resells outside brands. Stick to the Exclusives collection to stay in brand-designed territory.

name: Gantri
why: Sculptural 3D-printed lamps, each credited to an independent designer and printed in California.
watch: Plant-based plastic rather than metal or glass; the look is more modern than vintage.
